samples.text:
News is very important in our life because it tells us what is happening in the world. Some people think that news organisations must report only facts and journalists should not give their own opinion. I agree with this idea to a large extent.

The main reason is that people need correct information to make decisions. For example, before an election, people read the news to know about the candidates. If the journalist write his personal opinion, the readers can be influenced and they may vote for the person the journalist like, not the person they really prefer. This is dangerous for democracy. News should help people to think by themselves.

Another reason is that nowadays there are too much fake news and many people do not trust the media. When news is full of opinions, it is difficult for the readers to know what is true and what is only the idea of the writer. If news organisations report only facts, people will trust them more.

On the other hand, sometimes opinion can be useful. Some topics, like economy or politics, are very difficult to understand, and an expert journalist can explain what the facts means. However, I think this should be in a separate part, for example an opinion column, and it must be clear to the readers that it is not the news.

In conclusion, I mostly agree that news organisations should report only facts and not the opinions of their journalists, because people need true information and trust in the media. If opinions are included, they should be clearly separated from the news reports.

samples.text:
In an era of instant news and widespread misinformation, some people argue that news organisations should limit themselves strictly to reporting facts, without any personal opinion from journalists. While I agree that news reports should be as objective as possible, I disagree that opinion should never be included, as analysis plays an important role when it is clearly labelled.

There are good reasons to value factual reporting. Readers rely on the news to form their own views on political and social issues, and when a journalist's opinions are mixed into a report, the audience may be influenced without realising it. This is particularly concerning during elections or crises, when biased coverage can shape public opinion on a large scale. Strictly factual reporting also helps to rebuild trust in the media at a time when many people suspect that news outlets are pushing a particular agenda.

However, facts alone do not always tell the full story. A list of figures about inflation or a statement from a government minister may mean little to ordinary readers unless someone explains the context and possible consequences. Experienced journalists who have covered a subject for years is often well placed to offer this kind of insight. Removing all interpretation would leave audiences with information but little understanding.

The real problem, in my view, is not opinion itself but the failure to separate it clearly from news. Reputable newspapers usually distinguish between news articles and editorials or columns, allowing readers to know when they are reading an interpretation. Maintaining this distinction, and making it obvious on websites and social media, would address most of the concerns raised.

In conclusion, news reports should be based on facts, but I do not believe journalists' opinions should be banned entirely. Clearly labelled analysis and commentary help audiences to understand complex events and remain a valuable part of journalism.

samples.text:
Concerns about media bias and misinformation have prompted calls for news organisations to report nothing but verifiable facts, excluding the personal views of their journalists altogether. I agree that the core of news reporting should be factual and impartial, but I disagree that opinion should never appear, since informed commentary, when clearly identified, serves a valuable public function.

The argument for strict factual reporting is rooted in the democratic role of the press. Citizens depend on the news to understand events and hold those in power to account, and they are entitled to form their own conclusions. When commentary is woven into ostensibly neutral reports, readers may absorb a journalist's perspective without recognising it as such. This subtle blurring is arguably more damaging than openly partisan coverage, because it erodes the audience's ability to distinguish evidence from interpretation, and with it their trust in the media as a whole.

Yet it is naive to suppose that facts can be presented without any judgement. Deciding which stories to cover, which sources to quote and what context to include already involves editorial choices. Moreover, many issues, from climate policy to interest rates, are so complex that raw data offers little insight to non-specialists. A correspondent with years of experience can explain why an event matters and what its likely implications are, which enriches public understanding rather than distorting it.

The more sensible standard, therefore, is transparency rather than prohibition. News reports should strive for accuracy and balance, while analysis and opinion should be explicitly labelled and presented separately, as is the practice in most respected publications. The challenge in the digital age is to preserve this distinction when articles are shared on social media, often stripped of the labels that signal their purpose.

In conclusion, factual reporting should remain the foundation of journalism, but clearly marked opinion has a legitimate place. The priority should be to keep the two distinct, not to eliminate commentary entirely.
